newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: KERNOT SAYS WAY OPEN FOR GOVERNMENT TO APOLOGISE

Democrats leader Cheryl Kernot says a statement by the Federal government's Chief General Counsel, Henry Burmester, in relation to an apology to the stolen generation, raises questions about the government's credibility.
John Howard has argued that an apology outside Parliament could leave it liable to compensation.
But Mr Burmester told a Senate hearing it may be possible for the Government to word an apology without incurring legal liability.
Senator Kernot says the Prime Minister no longer has any legal excuse to avoid making an apology to the Stolen Generation.
WORKERS AT HUNTER VALLEY'S NUMBER ONE MINE WALK OFF JOB
Miners at the Hunter Valley's Number One mine, near Singleton, walked off the job at midnight after a breakdown in negotiations over an enterprise agreement.
The mine's general manager, Allan Davies, says he is deeply disappointed at the decision of the CFMEU and other unions to go ahead with the strike.
The unions and Hunter Valley Number One management met in the Industrial Commission today, but failed to resolve the dispute.
The matter will go before Mr Justice Boulton again tomorrow morning.
REPORT WARNS OF SYDNEY HOUSING BUST
The author of a report in Sydney says too many homes are being built in the city's inner-west in the lead-up to the Olympics, with the housing market in danger of over-heating.
The study by the University of Technology's Angleo Karantonis points to a pre-Olympics housing bust.
Mr Karantonis says foreign investors are most at risk of losing out from a downturn, if they continue to back new housing developments close to the Olympic site at Homebush.
GOVERNOR GENERAL EXPRESSES REGRET AT "AUSTRALIAN DISEASE"
Opening a melanoma conference at Sydney's Town Hall last night, the Governor General, Sir William Deane, said he regretted that skin cancer had become known as the "Australian disease".
Addressing world experts on melanoma, Sir William said it was significant that the conference was being held in Australia which has the world's highest incidence of the disease.
Sir William said because Australia had a population with many highly sun-sensitive skins coping with fierce ultraviolet rays, it was an appropriate human laboratory to combat the disease.
